definition: Data that comes in pairs: two measurements, such as height and mass, taken from each member of a sample.
A graph that plots each pair $(x, y)$ of bivariate data as one point, to show how the two variables are related.
How closely the points of a scatter diagram follow a straight line, described by direction (positive, negative or zero) and strength (strong, weak or none).
The number $r$, with $-1 \le r \le 1$, that measures the strength and direction of linear correlation only; $r$ near $0$ means no straight-line link, though the variables may still follow a curve.

The boundary value of a test statistic for a given significance level: correlation is significant when $\lvert r\rvert$ is greater than the critical value of $r$, and in a $\chi^{2}$ test $\mathrm{H}_0$ is rejected when $\chi^{2}$ is greater than its critical value.
A straight line drawn by eye that follows the trend of the points on a scatter diagram and passes through the mean point $(\bar{x}, \bar{y})$.
When a change in one variable directly produces a change in another; a correlation alone, however strong, does not show causation.
The least-squares line of $y$ on $x$, $y = ax + b$, used to predict $y$ from a value of $x$ inside the range of the data; it cannot reliably predict $x$ from $y$.
